deleteAccount.title: Delete your LifeLink account
deleteAccount.inAppStep1: Open LifeLink and go to the Me tab.
deleteAccount.inAppStep2: Tap Delete account and read what will be deleted.
deleteAccount.inAppStep3: Confirm, then sign in with Google once more. Your account is deleted straight away.
deleteAccount.noAppHeading: If you can no longer use the app
deleteAccount.noAppBody: Write to us from the email address of your Google account and ask for your LifeLink account to be deleted. We check that the request is really yours, delete the account, and reply to confirm — usually within 7 days.
deleteAccount.noEmailConfigured: The contact address for deletion requests has not been set up yet. Please use the steps in the app.
deleteAccount.whatDeleted: Deleted: your name, blood type, district, location, push token, and the phone numbers on requests you posted. Your name is removed from the public board.
deleteAccount.whatClosed: Closed: requests you posted that are still waiting or open. If you had accepted an open request, that acceptance is withdrawn.
deleteAccount.whatKept: Kept without your name: the fact that a request was made, answered or a donation was confirmed — so hospitals' statistics stay correct. Nothing kept can be traced back to you.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: LifeLink KH connects people in Phnom Penh who urgently need blood with nearby voluntary donors. It is free, it shows no ads, and it never sells or rents your information. This page says exactly what LifeLink collects, who can see it, and how to delete it.

sections.heading: Who we are
paragraphs: LifeLink KH is run by a small volunteer team in Cambodia. "We" below means that team. The app and this website use Google Firebase to store data, and Vercel to run the website.

sections.heading: What we collect
items: Your account: the name and email address of the Google or Facebook account you sign in with, and your preferred language.

If you register as a donor: your full name, blood type, district, the date you last gave blood (if you enter it), whether you are available to donate, your sex if you choose to give it (it sets how long you wait between donations), and — only if you allow it — your phone's location when you set up your donor profile.
If you post a request for blood: the patient's blood type, how many units, how urgent, the hospital, and the contact name and phone number you enter for donors to call.
When you answer a request: whether you accepted or declined, when, and your distance from the hospital.
When a donation is confirmed by our admin: the date, the hospital and the request it answered.
A notification token, so your phone can receive alerts. We do not collect your contacts, photos, messages or your location in the background, and there is no advertising or analytics tracking.

If you report a request: the reason you chose and any note you write. Only our admin sees it, and the family is not told who sent it. If you delete your account, your account and note are removed from the report; the reason is kept.

sections.heading: How we use it
items: To find donors whose blood type is compatible, who are eligible (90 days since their last donation for men, 120 days for women or if sex is not given) and who are near the hospital, and to send them an alert.
To tell the person who asked for blood that their request was approved, rejected, or accepted by a donor.
To show you when you can donate again.
So our admin can check that a request is genuine before any donor is alerted, and record donations the hospital confirms.
To count, without names, how many donors registered, how quickly requests were answered and how many donations happened.

sections.heading: Who can see what
items: Anyone, without signing in, can see the public board: open requests (blood type, units, urgency, hospital, time) and, for each request, a shortened name (for example "Nem S."), blood type and district of donors who accepted it. Requests waiting for review or rejected are not shown.
A donor who accepts a request can see the requester's contact name and phone number, so they can arrange the donation. Apart from the requester and our admin, nobody else can.

Your donor profile (blood type, sex, location, last donation) is visible only to you and our admin. Other users, including the families asking for blood, cannot see it. Matching reads it on our server.
Our admin can see everything above, to review requests, confirm donations and answer deletion requests.

Google (Firebase, sign-in, notifications), Facebook (if you sign in with it) and Vercel (the website) process data to provide their services to us. Their own privacy policies apply to what they do with it.

sections.heading: Where it is stored
paragraphs: Our database and server functions run in Google Cloud in Singapore. Sign-in is handled by Google and, if you use it, Facebook, which may process data in other countries. Data is encrypted on its way between your phone, the website and our servers.

sections.heading: How long we keep it, and deleting it
paragraphs: We keep your information while you have an account. You can delete your account at any time in the app: Me → Delete account. If you cannot use the app, see the deletion page linked below.

Deleting your account removes your profile, blood type, location, notification token and the phone numbers on requests you posted, and your name from the public board. Your open requests are closed, and an acceptance on an open request is withdrawn. We keep records that a request was made, answered or a donation confirmed, with your name and account removed, so that statistics stay correct; these cannot be traced back to you. Deleted data can remain in our backups for up to 7 days before it is gone.

sections.heading: Your choices
items: Location is optional. You can register as a donor without it; you are then matched by district.
You can turn notifications off in your phone's settings, and mark yourself unavailable in the app at any time.
You can correct your profile in the app, and ask us for a copy of your information using the contact below.

sections.heading: Safety
paragraphs: LifeLink never asks donors or families for money. Donate only at a hospital or blood center. LifeLink's count of days between donations is not medical advice; the hospital decides whether you can donate.

sections.heading: Age
paragraphs: LifeLink is for people aged 18 and over. We do not knowingly collect information from children. If you believe a child has created an account, contact us and we will delete it.

sections.heading: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: If we change what we collect or who can see it, we will update this page and its date. For a significant change, we will also tell you in the app.

download.title: Get the LifeLink app
download.intro: LifeLink is free. It is not on the Play Store yet, so you download it from here and install it yourself. It takes about a minute.
download.step1: Tap Download above and download the LifeLink APK file.
download.step2: Open the downloaded file. If Android says installing from this source is not allowed, tap Settings and turn on "Allow from this source" for your browser, then go back.
download.step4: Open LifeLink and sign in with Google.
download.warningHeading: "This app may be unsafe" — why you see it
download.warningBody: Android and Google Play Protect warn about every app that does not come from the Play Store. The warning does not mean something was found in LifeLink. Download it only from this page, and choose "Install anyway" if Play Protect asks.
download.updatesBody: The app tells you when a new version is available. Come back to this page, download it again and install it over the old one — you stay signed in and keep your history.

gettingBlood.title: How getting blood works
gettingBlood.subtitle: For families of patients, and for donors, in Cambodia
gettingBlood.intro: In Cambodia, most blood for patients comes from relatives and friends who donate. Here is what families and donors need to know.

sections.heading: Any blood type can help
items: Relatives and friends can donate at the hospital's blood bank or at the National Blood Transfusion Center, whatever their blood type.
Their blood goes into the tested stock, and the blood bank gives the patient the type they need.
Ask the hospital's blood bank how many donors they need from your family.

sections.heading: Blood is free
items: By national policy, blood is free to the patient. The hospital may charge a fee for testing and processing. Ask the hospital how much.
Never pay anyone for blood or for a donor. If someone offers to sell you blood, tell the hospital.
LifeLink never asks for money, from families or from donors.

sections.heading: Blood from close relatives
items: Do not arrange for a parent's, child's or sibling's blood to go straight to the patient. Let them donate to the blood bank. The hospital decides how blood from relatives is used.

sections.heading: Before you donate
items: You need to weigh at least 45 kg and usually be 18 to 60 years old.
Have a meal or snack in the 4 hours before, and drink plenty of water.
A standard donation in Cambodia is 350 ml. The whole visit is usually under an hour.

sections.heading: Wait before donating if you…
items: had a fever or felt ill in the last 2 weeks
took antibiotics in the last 2 weeks
had dengue or malaria in the last 6 months
got a tattoo, piercing or acupuncture in the last 12 months
are pregnant or breastfeeding, or gave birth in the last 6 months
had surgery or received blood in the last 12 months
Staff at the centre make the final check. If you are not sure, ask them before you donate.

sections.heading: Where to donate
items: National Blood Transfusion Center (NBTC): St 271, next to Khmer-Soviet Friendship Hospital, Phnom Penh. Walk-ins welcome.
Hospital blood banks and mobile blood drives also collect blood. Watch the Cambodia Blood Service page for dates.
After a donation, wait 3 months (men) or 4 months (women) before the next one. LifeLink counts this for you; the centre makes the final check.

gettingBlood.source: Based on Cambodia's national blood policy and WHO guidance. The hospital's blood bank and the NBTC have the final word on their own rules.
